parole.significato: hamster (any of various Old-World rodent species belonging to the subfamily Cricetinae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from East Slavic, from Old East Slavic хомѣкъ (xoměkŭ), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kāmjas (compare Latvian kãmis (“hamster”), Lithuanian kãmas (“rat”)). See further at Proto-Slavic *xoměstorъ.

parole.significato: courtyard (circumscribed area, often surrounded by a building or complex, that is open to the sky)
parole.testo: Borrowed from East Slavic, from Old East Slavic дѣтиньць, дитиньць, дѣтиниць (dětinĭcĭ, ditinĭcĭ, dětinicĭ). By surface analysis, dziedzina + -iec. Compare Belarusian дзяцінец, дзядзінец (dzjacinjec, dzjadzinjec), Russian дети́нец (detínec), Ukrainian дити́нець (dytýnecʹ). Piecewise doublet of dziec
Borrowed from East Slavic, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kolo. Cognate with Russian коля́ска (koljáska).

parole.significato: a type of porridge made from corn/maize or oat flour or, less commonly, wheat or rye flour
parole.testo: Borrowed from East Slavic, compare Ukrainian куліш (kuliš), Belarusian кулёш (kuljóš), Russian куле́ш (kuléš), кули́ш (kulíš), probably from Hungarian köles (“millet”).
From an East Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *oblava.

Uncertain. Possibly a back-formation from racuszek, a dialectal variant of raczuszek, itself a diminutive of rak (“crayfish”). Derivation from East Slavic cannot be ruled out. Compare regional Belarusian рачыха (račyxa) and dialectal Ukrainian гречух (hrečux).
Borrowed from East Slavic, from Old East Slavic роубєжь (rubežĭ), from Proto-Slavic *rǫbežь. Doublet of rąbież.
Borrowed from an East Slavic language. By surface analysis, rzezać + -uń. Doublet of rezun.

parole.significato: synonym of płyta (“slab”) (a thin piece of rock)
parole.testo: Borrowed from East Slavic. By surface analysis, skrzyżyć + -al.
Borrowed from an East Slavic language. Compare Ukrainian упир (upyr). Doublet of wampir and wąpierz.
From East Slavic, from Old East Slavic витязь (vitjazĭ), from Proto-Slavic *vitędzь, from Proto-Germanic *wīkingaz. Doublet of wiciądz (“hero, warrior”) and wiking (“Viking”).

parole.significato: whole burnt offering (a sacrifice to a deity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from East Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *žьrtva. Compare Russian же́ртва (žértva).
